prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map supports a coarse near-to-far layout: the close walls or doorway edges are bright in frames 1–3, while the seating and rear wall are darker and roughly 3–5 m from the camera wearer. The dog changes from about 2–3 m ahead in frame 3 to roughly 1 m in frame 4 and within about 0.5–1 m in frame 5, showing a clear approach as it moves from near the centre toward the right; the couch remains behind it by roughly 1–3 m. Bright lower-edge regions indicate surfaces or objects very near the wearer, including the visible hand in frame 1, and the right side of frame 4 is partly occluded by a close dark object in the RGB. This map makes the approach and foreground/background separation clearer than RGB alone, but its smooth gradients, blown-out boundaries, and inconsistent tones on the dog and furniture make metric distances and fine occlusion order unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map supports object-level positions: seating is detected toward the back in frames 2–4, the dog is near the centre in frame 3 and spans the lower-right foreground in frame 5, and a small ball lies low and slightly right of centre in frame 3. These masks help separate overlapping silhouettes and show the dog moving closer and rightward relative to the couch, from roughly 2–3 m away to within about 1 m, while the couch stays several metres behind. No person is reliably segmented, so facing direction, gaze, and interpersonal distances cannot be established; the dog’s orientation is only approximately sideways in frame 5. The map is highly unreliable semantically—walls or furniture are labelled “car,” “surfboard,” and “chair,” the dog becomes “cow,” masks disappear between frames, and partially visible or edge-clipped objects are poorly captured.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is entirely black across all five frames, so it provides no detected body or hand skeletons and supports no direct estimate of human position, facing direction, gaze, limb configuration, or reach. In the RGB, only the camera wearer’s hand is partly visible at the bottom of frame 1 and no other clear person appears, but neither that hand nor any body is represented in this map. Consequently, arm’s-reach relationships can only be inferred from the depth and RGB—most notably the dog entering within roughly 0.5–1 m in frame 5—and not from pose geometry. The blank result is useful mainly as evidence of detection failure or absence of a detectable pose, and it cannot describe approach, retreat, turning, occlusion, or interaction across the sequence.
